newsitem.title: UK: British share buyback ruling makes room for tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: British share buyback ruling makes room for tax cuts.

text.p: The British government's decision to cancel tax credits on share buybacks, announced on Tuesday, will give the coffers a timely boost and make more room for Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to cut income tax in the budget.

Clarke said in a statement the change would produce an estimated yield for the Exchequer of up to 400 million pounds ($625 million) a year, a useful inflow of cash to the still-strapped public finances.
He is under intense pressure from party colleagues to deliver generous tax cuts in the November budget and is eager to find any savings to help offset them.
"The Treasury is looking for anything that will help it reduce income tax without denting the PSBR profile," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.
He forecast Clarke may cut up to three pence off the 24 percent standard rate of income tax in November.
"They will be paid for through stronger economic growth next year, trimming back public spending relative to existing plans, and if the Treasury can find any other tax breaks to withdraw, it will."
Public spending has outpaced tax revenue to the tune of 13.37 billion pounds in the first five months of this fiscal year, largely due to a disappointing take of indirect tax (VAT).
Although VAT receipts are expected to recover later in the tax year, Clarke has had to revise upward his forecast for the Public Sector Borrowing Requirement to 27 billion pounds from 22.5 billion.
He has repeatedly stated he will only cut taxes if the country can afford it, but political pressures are mounting.

The ruling Conservatives are trailing opposition Labour by over 20 points in the opinion polls and, with the election due to be held by May 1997 at the latest, party colleagues are pressing Clarke to deliver a tax giveaway on November 26 to try and reverse their fortunes.
If Clarke can find any more tax loopholes to close to help offset income tax cuts, so much the better.
Analysts suggest Britain's tax breaks on profit-related pay may be next for the chop.
Under this scheme, firms are encouraged to make part of employees' pay directly related to company profits and the success of the scheme is proving expensive.

"That is costing the Treasury around 1.5 billion pounds per year at the moment and we are suggesting they think about reversing it," said Lucy Chennells, senior researcher at the Institute of Fiscal Studies, a leading think-tank.
The IFS is expected to recommend an orderly removal of the scheme when it presents its "green budget' proposals on Wednesday.
